messages.subject: Designing multi-species survey
messages.body_plain:
Hi to all,
I am the warden of a WWF Reserve in Italy, studying the bird community. I have a question regarding the design of a line transect survey of the nesting bird community, based on singing males.

Most of the books about bird censuses suggest to take at least two counts of the birds along the designed route, one for early, resident birds between March and April and one for late migratory birds in May/June. Bigby "Bird Census Techniques" example of using the Distance software shows a line transect repeated five times in the season, and says: "Although each transect was 1Km long, there were five visits. Effort (transect lenght) is therefore set at five km. This tells distance to divide the results by five".

Now  my question. Some birds sing only early in the season, while other bird arrive late and sing only in June and July. My guessing is that setting the same effort for all the bird species would give wrong densities, too low for the bird that sing only for a short time. Varying the effort so that for nuthatches, for example, that stop singing at mid april, I would set the effort to 1 (in a two repeated count), while for blackbird I would put it to two, is it correct?

Thank you very much in advance.

Guido Sardella

messages.body_plain:
Yes Guido, that is correct.  Of course you would exclude any detections made on the visit that does not contribute to the effort.  In the UK BBS, for each species, only either the early visit or the late visit is used, depending on species.  But if you're recording only singing males, and for species that actively sing both early and late, using the data from both early and late visits makes sense.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:

messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] right truncation
messages.body_plain:
You should not see this level of sensitivity to choice of truncation distance.  If 9 observations is 5% of your data, you have around 180 observations, and for good quality data, density estimates should be pretty insensitive to choice of data.

Things to consider:

1.       What model are you using for the detection function?  Do you get this sensitivity whatever model you use?

2.       You have 2 observations at 200m, none between 150m and 200m.  This suggestions rounding in the data.  Is there also rounding at shorter distances?  A moderate amount of rounding is generally not a problem, unless there is significant rounding to zero distance.  If you have a number of zeros in the data, avoid models that can fit a spike (negative exponential and hazard-rate).

3.       If there is rounding, choose a value for w that does not correspond to a favoured rounding distance (such as 200m).  Here, 175m or 225m might be a better choice, though if you have extreme heterogeneity in probability of detection among animals, you might want to consider truncating substantially more than 5% of your data.  See for example Borkin, K.M., R.W. Summers and L. Thomas. 2012. Distribution, density and stand-type preferences of wood ant Formica spp.nest mounts in a Scots pinewood. European Journal of Entomology.109: 47-53.  (http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/len/papers/BorkinEJE2012.pdf)

4.       If rounding is an issue in your data, consider revising field methods and observer training, and adopt technology that allows better estimates of distance (e.g. laser rangefinders).

Given a sample size of 180, I can’t see how truncation of just two observations at 200m can give rise to a halving of the density estimate, unless there are serious problems with the data.  If the problem is that some individuals are inherently much more detectable than others, then either use mcds methods if you have a covariate that explains this variability or truncate more of your data.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Hello all, I´m trying to assess if there are differences in the density of grassland shorebirds (Pluvialis dominica and Tryngites subruficollis) among 17 plots. I did repeated surveys (8 per plot), once each three days, to see changes in densities over time and relate this with invertebrates biomass changes.

So, I need to calculate the density per species in every survey (separating species for analysis). I don´t have enough observations por estimating the f(0) for each survey and nothing makes me think that f(0) changes over time in a plot. In fact, nothing makes me think that f(0) is different among plots either.

The approach I figured out is the following and wanted to share with the group and receive comments. First, adjust f(0) for both each plot and all the plots together, and comparing AIC decide if I should pool the data or adjust f(0) for each plot. If I decide to adjust f(0) for each plot, I would use all the observations of all the surveys per plot (i.e. repeated surveys) Once I have the f(0) for each plor (or all plots together), I would apply

D=E(n). f(0). E(s)/ 2L

for each survey (i.e. each count per 3 days).

I appreciate it if you could comment on this approach. Thanks.

Last, how can I set distance categories for visualise histograms?

Thanks a lot,

Joaquín Aldabe.

messages.body_plain:
Joaquin:

Thank you for the added piece of important information regarding your survey design.  Your use of boldface characters indicate the significance of the single transect per plot.

This creates threats to the inference you wish to make from your study.  Without spatial replicates within each of your plots you are missing one of the elements of variability in your plot-specific density estimate.  Uncertainty in each plot-specific estimate needs to incorporate uncertainty in the parameters of the fitted detection function as well as uncertainty in the number of birds you encountered on a specific transect.  Had your transect been in a different place in your plot, you would have encountered a different number of birds.  That element of variability is missing from your design and therefore from your density estimate.

Without that source of variation, precision in the estimates of density you produce will be understated and your inference about temporal differences in density will not be correct.  A further threat to the inference from your study may arise from pooling data, across either time or space or both in the estimation of f(0).  When data are pooled to produce a pooled estimate of f(0), there is no longer independence between the density estimates that use that 'shared' f(0).  Thereby you either lose replication in the number of plots you sampled (they are not independent) or lose independence between your temporally-spaced visits.  The latter messes with your ability to make contrasts between density estimates at different times because there is an induced dependency in those estimates caused by the estimate of f(0) the density estimates share.

Not a pleasant situation I'm afraid and not something that can be resolved in analysis I'm afraid.

Without spatial replicates within each of your plots you are missing one of the elements of variability in your plot-specific density estimate.  Uncertainty in each plot-specific estimate needs to incorporate uncertainty in the parameters of the fitted detection function as well as uncertainty in the number of birds you encountered on a specific transect.  Had your transect been in a different place in your plot, you would have encountered a different number of birds.  That element of variability is missing from your design and therefore from your density estimate.

A further threat to the inference from your study may arise from pooling data, across either time or space or both in the estimation of f(0).  When data are pooled to produce a pooled estimate of f(0), there is no longer independence between the density estimates that use that 'shared' f(0).  Thereby you either lose replication in the number of plots you sampled (they are not independent) or lose independence between your temporally-spaced visits. Hi everybody,

I wonder if there is a rule of thumb regarding the relationship between the size of the segment (when you split the transect in segments) and the cell size for the prediction grid.

There is a recommendation that the segment should have twice the ESW or the strip band width in length.

On the other hand, environmental covariables may come from different sources with different resolutions: for exampe, a Digital Elevation Model comes with a 90m resolution and NDVI data from MODIS comes in 250m resolution. Even when we can average this values under a segment of a larger size, one would expect that using a smaller grid cell size would produce a more precise abundance estimate, but surely there is a trade-off.

Any suggestions welcome...

mod1.var <- dsm.var.gam(mod1, pred.data = preddata.varprop,off.set = offset.varprop)

include a detection function in the analysis (effectively strip
transects). The plotting function was expecting a detection function to
tell it about the group size of the observations so they can be plotted.
I have modified dsm so this error doesn't occur again and this will be
in the next CRAN release of dsm.

via the following mechanism:

install.packages("devtools")
library(devtools)
install_github("DistanceDevelopment/dsm")

or use observation=FALSE in your call to plot, which will ignore that
part of the code:

plot(mod1.var, xlab = "Easting", ylab = "Northing",observation=FALSE)

Hope this helps!

best,

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Negative exponential and hazard-rate functions
messages.body_plain:
Samantha:

The arguments on this subject are more biological than mathematical.  At the heart of distance sampling is the idea that detectability diminishes as a function of distance from the transect.  However the rate of that diminution ought to be slow, at least initially.  This is what is called the shoulder criterion.  Detectability is unlikely to go from 1.0 on the trackline to 0.5 1m away from the trackline, which is a slightly exaggerated description of the behaviour of a negative exponential model.  The clue is in the name that detectability is falling off at an exponential rate.

There are few situations in the field in which this is plausible; if this is the shape of your histogram of detections, it is likely caused by rounding to zero or guarding the trackline.  Consequently the appropriate course of action is to remedy the data collection process rather than fit a model that is implausible for the detection decay process.

As you note, data with a spike at zero are notorious to fit; give rise to large (often implausible) density estimates; and estimate the fundamental parameter of distance sampling (hat{f(0)}) with very poor precision (revisit the shoulder criterion discussion).  Those are some of the reasons why the negative exponential is not recommended; and by extension some of the challenges associated with spiked data.
